newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN chief expects Iraq oil-food deal to be renewed.
newsitem.headline: UN chief expects Iraq oil-food deal to be renewed.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Friday he expected the Security Council to renew the "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq which expires in June.
Annan said he thought that member states would see the humanitarian need among Iraqi civilians and also take into account Baghdad's legal obligations to pay Gulf War reparations.

The United Nations gave Iraq clearance last December for limited exports under the oil-for-food scheme so it could import relief aid for its 20 million citizens living under U.N. trade sanctions imposed since Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990.
Under the renewable deal, Iraq can sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.
Annan, asked whether he expected Security Council members to approve extension of resolution 986, which contains the "oil-for-food" mechanism, told a news conference:
"There have been some delays in really getting the scheme off the ground. Food has begun flowing into Iraq.

"My own sense is that the food-for-oil scheme was introduced because the member states realised that the sanctions could be a blunt instrument and they did not want to hurt the population in Iraq, particularly the women and children.

"My own suspicion is that once the six months is over, since the condition that led to the passage of that resolution will still be relevant and compensations will still have to be paid, the Council will be inclined to extend it for another six months."
Annan, who succeeded U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in January, added: "It is regrettable that it took about six years for it (the deal) to get off the ground."
The U.N. Compensation Commission, set up by the Security Council, receives 30 per cent of revenue from the limited sale of Iraqi crude oil sold under the "oil-for-food deal".

Last month it paid out $144 million to some 57,636 successful claimants, the first payments funded by revenues from the deal and the most substantial to date. The money went to people in 63 countries who proved they were forced to leave Kuwait or Iraq or who had lost up to $100,000.
The Geneva-based U.N. reparations fund is handling $220 billion worth of claims filed by individuals, companies and governments against Baghdad for losses directly to due its invasion of Kuwait.
